quote: Machine learning, meanwhile, is producing a growing collection of techniques for specific kinds of problems, but as yet no general purpose algorithm for artificial intelligence. By bringing these two fields together, we can have both a high level architecture for an artificial general intelligence, and working algorithms for implementing many of the required components.
claim_summary: Talk abstract arguing that combining systems neuroscience with machine learning can give a high-level architecture for artificial general intelligence and working algorithms for many of its parts; notes there is as yet no general-purpose learning algorithm.
definition_note: artificial general intelligence, contrasted with techniques for specific kinds of problems
notes: Abstract of his talk at the Singularity Summit, San Francisco, 14-15 August 2010, read on the original Summit page through the Wayback Machine (first person: "In this talk I will outline the case for pursuing this approach"). Date: the Summit dates on the page; the day of his slot is not given, so month precision. This is the earliest dated statement found; the talk title is "Combining systems neuroscience and machine learning: a new approach to AGI" (the panel evidence used the later title "A systems neuroscience approach to building AGI"). Ambiguous field: endorsement. "we can have both a high level architecture for an artificial general intelligence" can be read as accepting that AGI can be built, but the words claim an architecture and algorithms for components, not that AGI will exist, so coded unexpressed (codebook: explicit endorsement required) with the route claim in claim_summary. "as yet no general purpose algorithm" raises capability_now and is coded disputed. The video is on YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=Qgd3OK5DZWI) but no transcript was read.

quote: We're many, many decades away from anything, any kind of technology that we need to worry about,
claim_summary: At a news conference on the Atari-playing system, says AI technology that people need to worry about is many decades away.
definition_note: "any kind of technology that we need to worry about"; the report frames it as AI one day taking over
notes: secondhand; basis: "We're many, many decades away"; TweakTown article by Michael Hatamoto, posted 2015-02-27, read on the Wayback Machine copy; it says he was "speaking during a recent news conference" and names washingtonpost.com as a source (not read). The news conference is the one for the Nature paper on the Atari-playing system (published 2015-02-25), so the words were said earlier that week: month precision. A14 ruling 11: "decades away" is accepts with a qualitative timeline. Ambiguous field: target_capability. The words name no capability, only technology "we need to worry about"; coded superintelligence because the report sets it against fears of AI taking over, but it could be read as broad_competence. Same quote continues: "But it's good to start the conversation now and be aware of as with any new powerful technology it can be used for good or bad."

quote: “We’re still decades away from anything like human-level general intelligence,” he reminds me. “We’re on the first rung of the ladder. We’re playing games.”
claim_summary: Says human-level general intelligence is still decades away and that current work, playing games, is the first rung of the ladder.
definition_note: human-level general intelligence; the profile glosses AGI as a general-purpose learning machine that can master any task from raw data
notes: basis: "We’re still decades away"; Observer (Guardian) profile by Clemency Burton-Hill, who interviewed him in his office; read at the original, quote verbatim. Date from the page's publication time. A14 ruling 11: "decades away" is accepts with a qualitative timeline. "We’re on the first rung of the ladder" raises capability_now (disputed). Context: said in reply to fears voiced by Hawking, Musk and Bostrom; he says alarmism is misplaced "not least because of the timescale" (reporter's paraphrase). Same piece: "One way of thinking of AGI is as a process that will automatically convert unstructured information into actionable knowledge."

quote: And so I think I would be very hesitant to bet against how far the universal Turing machine and classical computation paradigm can go. And my betting would be that all of, certainly what's going on in our brain, can probably be mimicked or approximated on a classical machine, not requiring something metaphysical or quantum.
claim_summary: Says he would bet that what goes on in the human brain can probably be mimicked or approximated on a classical computer, with nothing metaphysical or quantum required.
definition_note: what is going on in the brain mimicked or approximated on a classical machine
notes: basis: "my betting would be that all of, certainly what's going on in our brain, can probably be mimicked or approximated on a classical machine"; Lex Fridman podcast #299, "Demis Hassabis: DeepMind - AI, Superintelligence & the Future of Humanity". Read in Lexicap, a machine (speech-recognition) transcript published by Andrej Karpathy, through the Wayback Machine; the transcript has no speaker labels, but this is his answer about classical computation after Fridman's question. The words run across several timestamped lines on the page. Date from the episode page on lexfridman.com (published 2022-07-01). Endorsement: "my betting would be" is a bet, which counts as acceptance (codebook), though "probably" softens it; confidence medium for that and the machine transcript. Target broad_competence: matching what the brain does, not a named capability.

quote: "I don't see any reason why that progress is going to slow down. I think it may even accelerate. So I think we could be just a few years, maybe within a decade away."
claim_summary: Says AI progress shows no sign of slowing and may accelerate, so artificial general intelligence could be just a few years, maybe within a decade, away.
timeline_text: could be just a few years, maybe within a decade away
definition_note: the report glosses AGI as systems that think in similar but superior ways to humans
notes: secondhand; computed: 2023 + 10 (upper bound); basis: "we could be just a few years, maybe within a decade away"; The Independent (Anthony Cuthbertson), dated 2023-05-04, read on the Yahoo News syndicated copy; the remark was made at the Wall Street Journal's Future of Everything Festival "this week", so month precision. Original is the festival session (video, not read). A14 ruling 10: "could" and "maybe" hedge the date, so uncertain even though "I think" is present (the hedge decides). The same remark is quoted by AI Business on 2023-05-03 as "We could be just a few years, maybe within a decade, away" to AGI.

quote: “I think we’ll have very capable, very general systems in the next few years,” he added.
claim_summary: Says he expects very capable, very general AI systems within the next few years.
definition_note: "very capable, very general systems", said in the same remarks as the AGI timeline
notes: secondhand; basis: "I think we’ll have very capable, very general systems in the next few years"; AI Business article by Deborah Yao, 2023-05-03, reporting the Wall Street Journal Future of Everything Festival session; month precision because the article does not give the session day. Kept as its own row because it is a separate, unhedged claim from the hedged AGI date in hassabis-2023-01. Ambiguous field: target_capability. "very capable, very general systems" may mean less than AGI; coded broad_competence because it follows directly on the AGI timeline.

quote: I think there’s a lot of uncertainty over how many more breakthroughs are required to get to AGI, big, big breakthroughs — innovative breakthroughs — versus just scaling up existing solutions. ... But right now, I would not be surprised if we approached something like AGI or AGI-like in the next decade.
claim_summary: Asked how many years until AGI, says it depends on how many big breakthroughs are still needed, but he would not be surprised to approach something like AGI in the next decade.
timeline_text: would not be surprised if we approached something like AGI or AGI-like in the next decade
notes: computed: 2023 + 10 (upper bound); basis: "I think there’s a lot of uncertainty"; The Verge Decoder podcast, interview by Nilay Patel, transcript on theverge.com read at the original. Date from the page's publication time. Endorsement judgment: "I would not be surprised" is none of the acceptance words and is preceded by an explicit statement of uncertainty, so uncertain; confidence medium because it could be read as a soft acceptance. Same interview: he calls planning, memory and reasoning "vital for us to get to AGI".

quote: it’s something that we should consider, too, in the limit is what these systems can do and might be able to do as we get closer to AGI. We are nowhere near that now. So this is not a question of today’s technologies or even the next few years’, but at some point,
claim_summary: Explaining why he signed the extinction-risk statement, says the risks concern what systems might do as we get closer to AGI, that we are nowhere near that now, and that it is not a question for the next few years but for some later point.
timeline_text: not a question of today’s technologies or even the next few years’, but at some point
notes: The Verge Decoder podcast (Nilay Patel), same interview as hassabis-2023-03, a separate passage; read at the original. "We are nowhere near that now" denies that current systems are close to AGI (present_capability disputed, ruling 9); "at some point" is not an explicit claim that AGI will arrive, so endorsement unexpressed. Consequence coded existential because the passage explains his signing of the May 2023 statement on extinction risk (named just before the quote); agency can_influence from "we should consider" and, just after the quote, "we will need to think about those questions". Just before the quote: "I don’t think it’s likely, I don’t know on the timescales" (about the risk, not AGI arrival).

quote: Hassabis said the world was a long time away from AGI systems being developed but “we can see the path there, so we should be discussing it now”.
claim_summary: Says the world is a long time away from developing AGI systems but the path there can be seen, so it should be discussed now.
definition_note: the article glosses AGI as systems with human or above-human intelligence that could evade human control
notes: basis: "we can see the path there"; Guardian interview by Dan Milmo, global technology editor, ahead of the Bletchley Park summit; read at the original. Date from the byline (24 Oct 2023). Only the words in quotation marks are his; "a long time away" is the reporter's paraphrase, kept in timeline_text with that label. Endorsement accepts rests on his own words "we can see the path there". Agency can_influence from "we should be discussing it now". Contrasts with his May and July 2023 remarks (few years to a decade); recorded as reported.

quote: when we started DeepMind back in 2010, we thought of it as a 20-year project. And I think we’re on track actually, which is kind of amazing for 20-year projects because usually they’re always 20 years away. ... So I wouldn’t be surprised if we had AGI-like systems within the next decade.
claim_summary: Asked for his AGI timeline, declines to give specific numbers but says DeepMind was planned in 2010 as a 20-year project, that it is on track, and that he would not be surprised by AGI-like systems within the next decade.
timeline_text: 20-year project ... I think we’re on track ... wouldn’t be surprised if we had AGI-like systems within the next decade
notes: computed: 2010 + 20 (the 20-year project he says is on track; the "next decade" remark would give 2034 at most); basis: "I think we’re on track"; Dwarkesh Patel podcast, transcript on dwarkesh.com read at the original; date from the page. Just before the quote he says "I don’t have prescribed specific numbers to it because I think there’s so many unknowns and uncertainties." Ambiguous field: endorsement. "I think we’re on track" for a 20-year project from 2010 reads as acceptance of about 2030, while "I wouldn’t be surprised" and the refusal of specific numbers read as uncertain; coded accepts on the acceptance words, flagged ambiguous.

quote: I think that’s potentially possible. I think it partly depends on what we, as a society, decide to use the first nascent AGI systems or proto-AGI systems for. ... I could imagine these systems being quite good at designing and helping us build future versions of themselves, but we also have to think about the safety implications of that
claim_summary: Asked whether AGI would speed up further AI research, says it is potentially possible, depending on what society uses early AGI systems for, and that he can imagine such systems helping design and build future versions of themselves, with safety implications.
definition_note: "the first nascent AGI systems or proto-AGI systems"
notes: basis: "I think that’s potentially possible"; Dwarkesh Patel podcast, same interview as hassabis-2024-01, separate passage; read at the original. Question: whether once you have an AGI it speeds up further AI research over months and years. Ruling 12: "designing and helping us build future versions of themselves" does not say the systems improve themselves without people, so the lowest level the words support, si_assist, with ambiguous yes (target could be read as si_research). "potentially possible" and "could imagine" are hedges, so uncertain. Agency can_influence from "depends on what we, as a society, decide".

quote: My original ambition in AI is to build what we sometimes call artificial general intelligence, which is a system that can exhibit all the cognitive capabilities that humans can. ... There’s still that to build, and I think that would be one of the most consequential inventions humanity will ever invent.
claim_summary: Defines artificial general intelligence as a system with all human cognitive capabilities, says it is still to be built, and calls it potentially one of the most consequential inventions ever.
definition_note: a system that can exhibit all the cognitive capabilities that humans can
notes: Nobel Prize website interview transcript, recorded 6 December 2024 during Nobel Week in Stockholm (date from the page); read at the original. "There’s still that to build" says AGI does not exist yet (present_capability disputed, ruling 9); "would be one of the most consequential inventions" is conditional on its being built and states no arrival, so endorsement unexpressed. Consequences raised but their kind and valence not named. Omitted from the quote between the two sentences: "Then we know we have a truly general system at that point, a kind of Turing machine."

quote: My estimate is sort of 50% chance by in the next five years, so by 2030 let’s say. So I think there’s a good chance that that could happen. Part of it is what is your definition of AGI?
claim_summary: Asked about his estimate of AGI by 2030, gives about a 50% chance within five years, by 2030, and notes it depends on how AGI is defined.
timeline_text: sort of 50% chance by in the next five years, so by 2030 let’s say ... a good chance that that could happen
definition_note: matching the cognitive functions of the brain, consistently across the board rather than jagged
notes: computed: 2025 + 5; basis: "50% chance by in the next five years"; Lex Fridman podcast #475, official transcript on lexfridman.com read at the original (fetched in follow-up hassabis-075 while looking for episode #299); date from the page's publication time. Codebook: a stated probability of 50% or more is accepts. Ambiguous field: endorsement, because "that could happen" is a hedge on the same date (A15 ruling 2 would make it uncertain); 50% is exactly the threshold, so flagged rather than resolved. 2025 was NOT searched year by year (run stopped before the 2025 queries); this row comes only from a source already read.
